H.answer: The Supreme Court in Baker v. Carr (1962) (Document 5, ID: 369_0186-01) established that the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires that state legislative voting districts be substantially equal in population, but it did not explicitly use the term "one-person, one-vote" in this case. However, the principle of one-person, one-vote was later articulated and applied in subsequent cases such as Reynolds v. Sims (1964) and Wesberry v. Sanders (1964), which built upon the foundation laid in Baker v. Carr. In Baker v. Carr, the Court held that voters have standing to challenge the constitutionality of a state's apportionment plan and that the Equal Protection Clause is applicable to cases involving legislative apportionment. The Court's decision in Baker v. Carr paved the way for the development of the one-person, one-vote principle, which was later reaffirmed in cases such as Kirkpatrick v. Preisler (1969) (Document 7, ID: 394_0526-01) and Mahan v. Howell (1973) (Document 8, ID: 410_0315-01).

Carr (ID: 369_0186-01) did establish that voters have standing to challenge the constitutionality of state legislative voting districts, but the holding specifically stated that the appellants have standing to maintain the suit and that the 1901 statute constitutes arbitrary and capricious state action, offensive to the Fourteenth Amendment. However, the one-person, one-vote principle was indeed a key aspect of the case, as the Court held that the constitutional claim is, in substance, that the 1901 statute's apportionment of the members of the General Assembly among the State's 95 counties denies the equal protection of the laws accorded by the Fourteenth Amendment due to the debasement of their votes. The case is often cited for the principle of "one-person, one-vote," which requires that state legislative voting districts be substantially equal in population. (ID: 369_0186-01)
